lessons.intro: Every exercise in this course works the same way: you edit a file, save it, and read what comes back. This module covers that loop: printing a line, reading the output, and reading a compiler error.

steps.title: Save a file and read its output
steps.text:
A C# program is a list of **statements** that run from top to bottom.

```csharp
Console.WriteLine("Hello");
```

This is one statement. It prints the text between the double quotes, then ends the line. The semicolon `;` ends the statement.

When you save an exercise, the checker **compiles** your code, runs it, and compares the result with what the task asked for. Compiling means the C# compiler reads the whole file first. If it finds an error, nothing runs.

steps.title: Predict before running

steps.title: Repair the greeting

Save the starter as it is and read the error. A compiler error looks like this:

```text
Scratch.cs(1,34): error CS1002: ; expected
```

- `(1,34)` is the line and the column where the compiler noticed the problem.
- `CS1002` is the error code. Every compiler error has one.

Fix the line the error names, save again, and compare the output with the prompt.

steps.title: Run C# outside this checker
steps.text:
With the .NET SDK installed, these commands create and run a console program in a new folder:

```sh
dotnet new console -o FirstProgram
cd FirstProgram
dotnet run
```

`Program.cs` holds the code. Replace its contents with a print statement from this lesson and run it again. `FirstProgram.csproj` holds project settings, including the target .NET version. `dotnet build` compiles without running. A project compiles its C# files together, so types in another `.cs` file can be used from Program.cs.

The short form used here has **top-level statements**. In a new console project, common namespaces such as `System` are imported automatically, which makes `Console` available. A namespace groups type names. `using System;` imports its names, and `System.Console.WriteLine("Hello");` uses the full name. Later exercise wrappers supply imports and an entry point so you can focus on one skill at a time.

lessons.intro: A program keeps its data in named **variables**. In C# every variable has a **type** that says what kind of value it can hold. This module covers whole numbers, numbers with a fraction, text and true/false values, and the arithmetic and text building every later module uses.

steps.title: Give a value a name and a type
steps.text:
A variable is a name for a value. In C# the type comes first:

```csharp
int temp = 4;          // a whole number
double price = 2.5;    // a number with a fraction
string city = "Oslo";  // text, in double quotes
bool raining = true;   // true or false
```

- Read `=` as "gets". `int temp = 4;` makes a variable named `temp` that holds whole numbers and gives it 4.
- A semicolon ends each statement, and statements run from top to bottom.
- A variable can get a new value later. `temp = temp + 1;` works out the right side first, then stores the result in `temp`.

steps.title: Choose a numeric type
steps.text:
Use `int` for whole-number counts, `double` for approximate fractional measurements, and `decimal` for decimal arithmetic such as money: `decimal price = 4.50m;`. The `m` suffix makes a decimal literal. Decimal cannot represent every fraction exactly, but values such as 0.1 have an exact decimal representation. Avoid mixing decimal and double without an explicit conversion.

An int has a finite range, from -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647. Use `long` for larger whole numbers. `checked(total + extra)` throws on integer overflow instead of allowing the result to wrap around.

steps.title: Divide two whole numbers
steps.text: `+`, `-` and `*` work as in arithmetic. Division depends on the types. When both sides are `int`, `/` gives a whole number and drops the fraction, and `%` gives the remainder. Predict the three lines before running.

steps.title: Convert before you divide
steps.text:
An `int` fits in a `double` with no extra code, as `double exact = slices;` showed. You can also convert in place with a **cast**: put the type in brackets before the value.

```csharp
double share = (double)slices / people;    // 3.5
double late = (double)(slices / people);   // 3
```

The order matters. The first line converts `slices`, then divides, so the fraction is kept. The second divides two ints first, which drops the fraction, and only then converts 3 to a `double`.

steps.title: Let the compiler pick the type, and build text
steps.text:
`var` asks the compiler to work out the type from the first value (**inference**). `var city = "Oslo";` means exactly the same as `string city = "Oslo";`. The type is still fixed.

A `$` before the opening quote makes an **interpolated string**: each `{name}` inside it is replaced by that value. Without the `$`, the braces are ordinary text. You can also join text with `+`.

lessons.intro: A program becomes useful when it can choose. This module covers `if` and `else`, the comparison operators, and combining true/false values with **and**, **or** and **not**.

steps.title: Compare, then choose
steps.text:
A comparison produces a `bool`. `cars > spaces` is true when `cars` is larger.

| Operator | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `==` | equal |
| `!=` | not equal |
| `<`, `<=` | less than, less than or equal |
| `>`, `>=` | greater than, greater than or equal |

An `if` statement runs its block only when the condition in the brackets is true. `else if` tries another condition when the ones above were false. `else` runs when none matched. Only one block in the chain runs.

Two strings are equal with `==` when they hold the same characters, and `""` is a real string with no characters in it.

steps.title: Which branch runs?
steps.text: Read the `if` chain and predict the first line of output.

steps.title: Combine conditions
steps.text:
- `&&` means **and**: true only when both sides are true.
- `||` means **or**: true when at least one side is true.
- `!` means **not**: it flips true and false.

`&&` skips its right side when the left is false. `||` skips it when the left is true. This is **short-circuit evaluation**. `count != 0 && total / count > 2` avoids dividing by zero. Use parentheses to make mixed conditions clear.

Predict the last two lines.

lessons.intro: A **method** packages steps under a name so they can be used again with different values. This module covers parameters, return values and **scope**: which names exist where.

steps.title: Parts of a method
steps.text:
```csharp
int AddHours(int hours, int extra)
{
    int total = hours + extra;
    return total;
}
```

- `int` before the name is the **return type**: the kind of value the method gives back.
- `hours` and `extra` are **parameters**: names for the values a caller passes in.
- `return` sends a value back to the caller and ends the call.
- A method that gives nothing back has the return type `void`.
- A conditional expression chooses one of two values: `condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse`. For example, `hours > included ? hours - included : 0` can be returned directly.
- When the body is a single expression you can write it with `=>`: `int Twice(int n) => n * 2;`
- A name declared inside a method's braces, such as `total`, exists only there. That region is the name's **scope**. Each call gets its own fresh parameters and local variables.

In exercises your methods go inside a class the checker supplies, so each one starts with `public static`. `public` lets other code call it. `static` means it is called by name, without an object. The Classes module explains both.

lessons.intro: Most programs work on many values at once. This module covers **arrays**, which have a fixed length, `List<T>`, which can grow, and the **loops** that visit each item.

steps.title: Arrays and loops
steps.text:
An array holds a fixed number of values of one type.

```csharp
int[] minutes = { 30, 15, 45 };
```

- Positions (**indexes**) start at 0, so `minutes[0]` is 30 and `minutes[2]` is 45.
- `minutes.Length` is the number of items.
- Reading a position that does not exist, such as `minutes[3]`, stops the program with an `IndexOutOfRangeException`.

A `foreach` loop runs its block once for each item, in order. A variable declared before the loop can collect a result across the runs.

steps.title: Trace a running total
steps.text: Follow `total` through each run of the loop, then predict the three lines.

steps.title: Lists that grow
steps.text:
A `List<T>` holds items of type `T` and can change size.

- `new List<string>()` creates an empty list of strings. `new List<int> { 4, 9 }` creates one with two items.
- `Add` appends an item. `Count` is the number of items (an array uses `Length`).

A `for` loop counts with a variable:

```csharp
for (int i = 0; i < songs.Count; i++) { ... }
```

It runs with `i` equal to 0, 1 and so on, and stops when `i` reaches `Count`. `i++` adds 1 to `i`. Use `for` when you need the position, and `foreach` when you only need the item.

steps.title: Repeat until a condition changes
steps.text: Use `while` when the number of repetitions is not known in advance. It tests its condition before each run. `break` exits the nearest loop immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current run and moves to the next condition test. Make sure a while loop changes something its condition uses, or it can run forever.

lessons.intro: A **class** groups data with the methods that work on it. This module covers properties, constructors and instance methods, and what happens when two variables refer to the same object.

steps.title: A class is a blueprint
steps.text:
A class describes one kind of thing. `new Book("Dune", 400)` creates an **object** from it.

- A **property** is a named value on each object. `public string Title { get; private set; }` can be read by any code and changed only inside the class.
- `public int Pages { get; }` is a get-only auto-property. It can be initialized at its declaration or in the constructor, then read but not reassigned.
- A property can work out its value each time it is read: `public bool Long => Pages > 500;`
- The **constructor** has the same name as the class. It runs once, when the object is created, and gives the properties their first values.
- A method without `static` belongs to one object and uses that object's own properties.

steps.title: Fields, access and static
steps.text:
A **field** stores data directly, as in `private int visits;`. A property exposes reads or writes through `get` and `set`, and can validate or compute a value. `private` limits access to the containing type. `public` allows access from other code. `protected` also allows derived classes to access a member.

An instance member uses one object's data, such as `book.Title`. A `static` member belongs to the type, such as `Math.Max(3, 5)`. A static method has no current object, so it needs an object passed in before it can read that object's instance members. `this` refers to the current object inside an instance member.

lessons.intro: Some types exist to carry data. This module compares ordinary classes, structs and record classes, including what assignment and `with` copy, and how equality works.

steps.title: A record carries data
steps.text:
`record Movie(string Title, int Minutes);` declares a record in one line. It gets a constructor with those two parameters and a property for each.

- This positional record class gets **init-only** properties: their values can be assigned during initialization, but not afterwards. A record can also declare properties with `set`, so records are not always immutable.
- To change something, make a copy with `with`: `first with { Minutes = 45 }` is a new `Movie` with the same `Title` and a different `Minutes`.
- Two records compare equal with `==` when their runtime types and stored members compare equal. A list member compares by reference, not by its contents.
- Printing a record shows its type name and its values.

steps.title: Copy with a change
steps.text: `second` is made from `first` with one value changed. Predict the first line of output.

steps.title: Value or reference
steps.text:
C# has value types and reference types. The table shows their default behavior. Classes can overload `==`, as `string` does, so the declared type matters.

| Kind | Assignment copies | `==` compares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `struct`, like `int` (a **value type**) | the whole value | (needs its own `==`) |
| `class` (a **reference type**) | the reference: both names refer to one object | the references: two separate objects are not equal, even with the same data |
| `record` (a record class) | the reference | the stored members |

So `Size b = a;` gives `b` its own copy when `Size` is a `struct`, and two `new Box()` objects are not equal when `Box` is a class.

steps.title: A copy can still share data
steps.text: `with` makes a **shallow copy**: it copies each member. A member holding a reference still points at the same object. A struct with a list member has this same issue on assignment. `record struct` is a value type with record equality, unlike the record classes above.

lessons.intro: Sometimes there is no value: a person with no nickname, a library book with no due date. C# calls that `null`. This module covers marking a value that may be missing, checking it before use, and supplying a fallback.

steps.title: null means no value
steps.text:
`null` means a variable refers to nothing. `string? nickname = null;` declares a string that may be missing. The `?` after the type tells readers and tools that `null` is allowed here, and editors use it to warn you when you use such a value without a check.

- Using a member of `null`, such as `nickname.Length`, stops the program with a `NullReferenceException`. Test first with `nickname == null` or `nickname != null`.
- `??` supplies a fallback: `nickname ?? "Guest"` is `nickname` when it has a value and `"Guest"` when it is `null`.
- `?.` reads a member only when there is a value: `nickname?.Length` is `null` when `nickname` is `null`, and nothing is thrown.

steps.title: Numbers that can be missing
steps.text:
An `int` always holds a number and can never be `null`. When a number may be missing, use `int?`, a different type that holds either an `int` or `null`.

```csharp
int? due = null;
Console.WriteLine(due.HasValue);   // False
due = 0;
Console.WriteLine(due ?? -1);      // 0
```

- `HasValue` is false while the value is `null`.
- After `due = 0;` it holds a real 0, so `??` keeps it. Like empty text, zero is a value.

lessons.intro: A list finds items by position. A `Dictionary` finds a value by its key, and a `HashSet` keeps each value only once. This module covers both, including what happens when a key is missing.

steps.title: Find a value by its key
steps.text:
A `Dictionary<string, int>` stores pairs: a `string` **key** and an `int` value for it.

- `votes["Ana"] = 2;` stores 2 under the key `"Ana"`. It adds the key if it is new and replaces the value if the key exists.
- `votes["Ana"]` reads the value. Reading a key that is not there stops the program with a `KeyNotFoundException`.
- To be safe, ask first with `ContainsKey`, or use `TryGetValue`: `votes.TryGetValue("Cy", out int found)` returns true and puts the value in `found` when the key exists, and returns false when it does not. `out` marks a variable that the method fills in.
- `Count` is the number of keys.

- `Contains` tests for a value, and `Count` is the number of different values.

outcomes.can: Filter and transform a list with Where and Select.

lessons.intro: Filtering, transforming and counting come up so often that C# has a set of methods for them, called LINQ. This module covers lambdas, the most used LINQ methods, and the fact that a query does not run until its results are read.

steps.title: A lambda is a small method
steps.text:
A **lambda** is a method written in place, without a name. `movie => !movie.Watched` takes one movie and returns whether it is still unwatched. The part before `=>` is the parameter, and the part after it is the result.

LINQ methods take lambdas:

| Method | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `Where` | keeps the items for which the lambda returns true |
| `Select` | replaces each item with the lambda's result |
| `Count()`, `Any()` | counts the items, or says whether there is at least one |
| `Sum` | adds up a number taken from each item |

The methods chain: the result of one is the input of the next.

steps.title: A query runs when it is read
steps.text:
`Where` and `Select` do not do their work when you call them. They return a description of the work, called a **query**. Its type is `IEnumerable<T>`, which means something you can loop over. Lists and arrays fit that type too.

- The query runs each time something reads it: a `foreach`, `Count()` or `ToList()`. This is called **deferred execution**.
- `ToList()` runs the query now and stores its results in a new, mutable list. Adding items to the source later does not add them to this list. Reference-type items can still be shared between the two lists.
- `ToDictionary` does the same into a dictionary, from one lambda for the key and one for the value.

outcomes.can: Implement an interface and use the type through it.

lessons.intro: Different types can often be used the same way: several places to read items from, several kinds of notice. This module covers interfaces, which state what a type can do, and inheritance, where one type builds on another.

steps.title: An interface is a contract
steps.text:
An **interface** lists members without bodies. `interface ISource` says that any source has a `Name` and a `Count` method.

- A class takes on the contract by naming the interface after a colon, as in `class FixedSource : ISource`, and must then provide every member. Having matching members is not enough: the class has to name the interface.
- A variable of type `ISource` can hold any object whose class implements it. Code written against `ISource` works with all of them, including classes written later. A loop over a `List<ISource>` calls each object's own `Name` and `Count` without knowing its class.

steps.title: A class can build on another
steps.text:
`class UrgentNotice : Notice` makes `UrgentNotice` a kind of `Notice`. It gets `Title` and `Text` from `Notice` (**inheritance**).

- `: base(title)` after the constructor passes the title on to `Notice`'s constructor.
- A method marked `virtual` in the base class may be replaced, and the derived class replaces it with `override`.
- Without `override`, a method with the same name only hides the base one, and a call through a `Notice` variable runs the base version.
- Records can inherit the same way: `record Arrived(int Count) : Update;`
- A type marked `abstract` cannot be created itself. It exists only to be inherited from.

lessons.intro: Code often has to ask two questions at once: what kind of value is this, and what is inside it? Pattern matching answers both in one step. This module covers the is test, switch expressions, type patterns and property patterns, using kitchen orders as data.

steps.title: Test a type and name the result
steps.text:
A **pattern** is a test that a value either matches or does not. The simplest is a type pattern: `update is Finished f` asks whether `update` is a `Finished` record. When it is, `f` is that same object seen as a `Finished`, so `f.Title` is available.

A **switch expression** tries several patterns in order and produces a value:

```csharp
string text = update switch
{
    Waiting w => $"Place {w.Place}",
    Finished f => f.Title,
    _ => "Unknown"
};
```

- Each arm is `pattern => result`, with a comma between arms. The first arm that matches wins.
- The discard `_` matches anything, so it goes last.
- Without a last arm that catches the rest, the compiler warns that the switch does not handle every input (CS8509). A value that then matches no arm throws `SwitchExpressionException` when the program runs.

steps.title: Test what is inside
steps.text:
A **property pattern** tests values inside an object.

- `{ Minutes: 0 }` matches when the `Minutes` property equals 0.
- A **relational pattern** compares: `{ Minutes: < 30 }` matches any value below 30.
- One pattern can test several properties: `{ Urgent: true, Minutes: > 60 }`.
- A property pattern can follow a type: `Finished { Minutes: 0 } f`.

Order matters, because the first match wins. Put the most specific arm first.

lessons.intro: Some failures are bugs, and some are expected: text that is not a number, a store that is offline. This module covers throwing and catching exceptions, and returning a result value when a failure is a normal outcome.

steps.title: Throw and catch
steps.text:
An **exception** is an object that reports a failure. `throw new ArgumentException("Minutes cannot be negative.");` stops the current method at once and passes the exception to its caller. If nothing catches it, the program stops.

- A `try` block marks code that may fail. A `catch` block after it runs only when an exception of the named type is thrown inside the `try`, and the rest of the `try` is skipped.
- `catch (FormatException)` catches that type and any derived exception types. Naming a variable, as in `catch (ArgumentException error)`, lets you read `error.Message`.
- Catch the most specific type you can handle. `catch (Exception)` catches everything, including bugs you would want to see, so it is rarely the right choice.
- Some built-in methods throw: `int.Parse("soon")` throws a `FormatException` because the text is not a number.

steps.title: Expected failures can be values
steps.text:
An exception suits a failure the caller is not expected to handle on every call, such as a broken promise about the input. When failure is a normal outcome, a return value is often clearer.

- A **result type** holds either the answer or the reason there is none, for example `record Parsed(bool Ok, int Minutes, string Error);`. The caller checks `Ok` before using the answer. This record makes failure visible but does not force the caller to check it.
- Built-in methods offer the same choice: `int.TryParse(text, out int value)` returns false for bad text instead of throwing.

steps.title: Release a resource on every path
steps.text:
Some objects hold files, connections or other resources. They implement **IDisposable**, an interface with a `Dispose()` method that releases the resource. Garbage collection reclaims managed memory, but it does not replace timely disposal.

```csharp
using var reader = LocalReader.Open(key);
return reader.Read();
```

This `using` is a declaration, different from a namespace import. It calls Dispose when the scope exits, including when Read throws or return runs. A `using (var reader = LocalReader.Open(key)) { ... }` statement gives the reader a smaller scope.

For cleanup that needs more control, put it in a `finally` block after `try` and any `catch` blocks. Finally runs on ordinary scope exit, including return and exception unwinding. A bare `throw;` inside a catch rethrows the current exception while preserving its original stack trace. Do not catch a failure just to silently return a success-looking value.

lessons.intro: A method that returns the first item of a list should work for a list of anything, and give back that same kind of thing. Generics let you write it once. This module covers generic methods, generic types and constraints.

steps.title: A type that the caller chooses
steps.text:
`T FirstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback)` is a **generic method**. `T` is a **type parameter**: a placeholder that each call fills in.

- Called with a `List<int>`, `T` is `int`, so the fallback must be an `int` and the result is an `int`. Called with a `List<string>`, the same code returns a `string`.
- The compiler works `T` out from the arguments, so you rarely write it yourself. One call has one `T`.
- A type can be generic too. `record Pair<T>(T First, T Second);` holds two values of one type, whichever type the code that uses it picks.
- `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` are generic types you have used already.

steps.title: Ask for an ability
steps.text:
Inside a generic method you know nothing about `T`, so you cannot compare two `T` values with `>` or call methods on them. A **constraint** states what `T` must be able to do.

```csharp
T Larger<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T> => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;
```

- `where T : IComparable<T>` accepts only types that can be compared with themselves, which includes `int` and `string`.
- Then `a.CompareTo(b)` is allowed. It returns a number above 0 when `a` comes after `b`, 0 when they are equal, and a number below 0 when `a` comes before `b`.

lessons.intro: Reading a file, a database or a network takes time. C# represents work that finishes later as a Task. This module covers `async` methods, `await`, choosing sequential or concurrent reads, cancellation, and failures. Every source here is local, so nothing depends on network access or measured delays.

steps.title: A Task is a result that comes later
steps.text:
A `Task<int>` represents an operation that may be pending, already finished, canceled, or failed. `await` gives you its int on success. Awaiting an incomplete task suspends this async method without blocking the current thread. Awaiting an already completed task can continue immediately.

- The methods here use `async Task` for no result and `async Task<T>` for a result. Inside an async Task<T> method, return a plain T. C# completes the task with that value. Avoid async void except for event handlers: callers cannot await it or handle its failures through a returned task.
- By convention the names of such methods end in `Async`.
- While a method waits at an `await`, the program is free to do other work, which is the point of writing code this way.
- A task's `Result` also waits, but it blocks the whole thread until the task is done. Prefer `await`.

outcomes.can: Use expected and actual values to find the input that exposes a bug.
Write a check that passes correct code and fails faulty code.

lessons.intro: A check calls code with a known input and compares what comes back with what should come back. This module covers reading a failed check, choosing the input that exposes a bug, and writing a check of your own.

steps.title: Expected and actual
steps.text:
Every check has an input, an **expected** result and an **actual** result.

- The expected result comes from the rule the code is meant to follow. The actual result is what the code returned.
- When they differ, the check has failed, and the input tells you which call to trace.
- The most useful inputs sit at an **edge**, where the rule changes its answer. For "three or more", the edge is exactly 3. A bug at an edge is easy to miss with inputs far away from it.

steps.title: Find the failing input
steps.text: `AtLimit` should return true when `count` has reached the limit or passed it. Predict the three lines, then decide which call shows the bug.

steps.title: A check is code too
steps.text:
A method can receive another method as a parameter. `Func<int, int, bool>` is the type of a method that takes two ints and returns a `bool`. The last type in the list is the return type. A lambda such as `(count, limit) => count >= limit` fits it.

- A check written this way takes a **candidate**, calls it with chosen inputs, and returns true only when every result matches what is expected.
- A good check returns true for correct code and false for the faulty versions you know about.
- A check kept to make sure a fixed bug stays fixed is called a **regression check**.

steps.title: Run the check on two candidates
steps.text: `Check` is given a correct candidate, then a faulty one. Predict the two lines of output.

steps.title: Repair an interval
steps.text: The new rule has two boundaries with different meanings. Use the failing inputs to repair both, including an empty interval.

steps.title: Write a check that finds a faulty count
steps.text: This time you write the check. It is run against a correct candidate and against faulty ones.

questions.prompt: Which call shows the bug?

choices.feedback: It prints True, and the rule also expects true for 4.

The rule expects True, True, False, and the code prints True, False, False. Only the call at the edge disagrees: 3 has reached a limit of 3, but the code uses `>`, which is false for equal values. The calls with 4 and 2 give the right answer with either operator, so they cannot tell the faulty code from the fixed code.
It prints False, and the rule also expects false below the limit.

questions.prompt: What are the two lines of output?

choices.feedback: The check includes the edge input (3, 3) with the expected result true. The first candidate returns true there and false for (2, 3), so the check passes. The second returns false at the edge, so the check fails. Without the (3, 3) case both candidates would pass, and the check would be worthless for this bug.
The second candidate returns false for (3, 3), where true is expected.
The first candidate returns true for (3, 3) and false for (2, 3), which is what is expected.
